title: HFNC flow versus delivered FiO2 at high inspiratory demand
subtitle: Cannula flow titration and effective FiO2 delivery during high inspiratory demand
ruleBasedNote: HFNC room-air dilution, dead-space washout (up to 50 mL), and continuous airway pressure (0.05 cmH2O per L/min) are rule-based approximations in Engine v1.

patient.summary: A 60-year-old tachypnoeic patient with hypoxic acute respiratory failure generating vigorous inspiratory effort and high peak inspiratory flow supported on high-flow nasal cannula.

prediction.question: When HFNC gas flow is escalated from 20 to 60 L/min while keeping the blender FiO2 setting at 0.80, how do delivered FiO2, PaO2, and airway pressure respond?

whatToLookAtHint: Observe the effective delivered FiO2, arterial oxygen tension (PaO2), and positive airway pressure generated at the nares.

reflection.question: Why does escalating cannula flow from 20 to 60 L/min substantially increase delivered FiO2 and PaO2 despite no change in the blender oxygen setting?

options.text: The tachypnoeic patient's peak inspiratory demand exceeds 20 L/min, entraining ambient room air (FiO2 0.21) around the prongs; increasing gas flow to 60 L/min matches peak demand and eliminates room-air dilution.
60 L/min increases gas kinetic energy, doubling oxygen solubility in pulmonary capillary plasma.
High flow induces reflex pharyngeal narrowing that traps 100% oxygen inside the glottic aperture.
Venturi blenders automatically calibrate to higher oxygen concentrations when backpressure rises.

reflection.explanation: Tachypnoeic patients with vigorous inspiratory efforts generate peak inspiratory flows (PIF) that can exceed 50-60 L/min. When HFNC flow is set to only 20 L/min, the remaining 30-40 L/min of inspiratory gas is entrained room air (21% O2) drawn through the mouth and around open nasal prongs. This dilutes the effective delivered FiO2 down to ~0.41. Escalating cannula flow to 60 L/min matches peak inspiratory flow, suppressing room-air entrainment so delivered FiO2 reaches the set 0.80, increasing alveolar PAO2 and arterial PaO2 (from ~75 to ~107 mmHg). Additionally, 60 L/min generates ~3 cmH2O of continuous airway pressure.

evidence.claim: Delivered FiO2 with open-system nasal cannulae falls below blender settings whenever patient peak inspiratory flow exceeds delivered cannula flow due to room air entrainment.
evidence.source: Nishimura M. High-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy in adults. J Intensive Care 2015; 3:15.

evidence.claim: High-flow nasal cannula generates flow-dependent positive airway pressure and anatomic dead space washout in adult patients.
evidence.source: Ritchie JE, Williams AB, Gerard C, Hockey H. Evaluation of a humidified nasal high-flow oxygen system, using normal volunteers. Intensive Care Med 2011; 37(5):780-786.
